title: Soil water retention

definition.text: A soil's ability to take in water and hold much of it against the pull of gravity.

facts.text: Soils keep taking in water until they are full, or until the rate at which their pores can pass water on is exceeded.
Some water drains by gravity to streams, but much is retained, and plants and other organisms use much of what stays.
Retention follows particle size: water clings more tightly to fine clay particles than to coarse sand grains, so clays hold more water while sands let it pass more easily.
Clay type, organic content and soil structure also affect how much water a soil retains.
Roughly, an agricultural topsoil is 25% water, 25% air, 45% mineral and 5% other, though its water ranges from about 1% to 90%.
Retained water supplies plants between refills; in temperate Victoria, Australia, water stored in wet winters carries most perennial plants through dry summers.
Water neither retained nor used by plants can move down to the water table as recharge, while a soil already at field capacity can block infiltration and increase overland flow.
Saturated soils can become unstable and fail by mass movement, so soil water concerns geotechnicians and soil conservationists.

title: Soil moisture and climate
article: Soil water (retention)#Soil water retention and climate

definition.text: The link between soil water and climate: soil moisture shapes a soil's thermal properties and the persistence of surface temperature and rainfall.

facts.text: Wetter soil warms and cools more slowly under the same heating, because water has roughly double the heat capacity of soil.
Through soil temperature, moisture affects biological triggers such as seed germination, flowering and the activity of soil fauna.
Climate modelling by Timbal and colleagues in 2002 linked soil moisture to the persistence and variability of surface temperature and precipitation in Australia.
Soil water matters for climate modelling and weather prediction, and the Global Climate Observing System lists it among its 50 Essential Climate Variables.

definition.text: The water held in a soil, measured by volume or by weight.

facts.text: Water that enters a field leaves it as surface runoff, as drainage through the soil, by evaporation from the surface or by transpiration from plants.
Water shapes soil formation, structure, stability and erosion, but its main importance is for plant growth.
Plants need water because it makes up 80–95% of their protoplasm, carries nutrients as a solvent, and keeps them upright through turgor.
In a loam, solids take up half the volume, gas a quarter and water a quarter, of which only about half is available to most plants.
Water moves in soil under gravity, osmosis and capillarity; entering water drives air out of macropores and can burst air-filled aggregates, a process called slaking.
Roots empty the largest pores first; water in the smallest pores clings so tightly to particles that roots cannot take it, so availability depends strongly on texture.
Moving water dissolves mineral and organic solutes and colloids and redeposits them lower in the profile, a process called leaching.
Soil moisture is measured in place with probes such as capacitance and neutron probes, or estimated by remote sensing.

definition.text: The two modes of water movement in soil: saturated flow, pushed by gravity and pressure in wet soil, and unsaturated flow, pulled by capillarity toward drier soil.

facts.text: Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to field capacity, gravity and differences in water pressure push water away from where it was applied; this is saturated flow.
At higher suctions, water's adhesion to soil solids sets up a suction gradient that pulls water from wetter to drier soil and from macropores to micropores.
Unsaturated flow moves water at most about 2.5 cm a day, so roots keep dying back and growing toward moister soil.
As soil dries its connected wet pathways shrink, so unsaturated hydraulic conductivity depends on water content and falls in a very non-linear way as soil dries.
Six factors control infiltration and movement: texture, structure, organic matter, depth to impervious layers such as hardpans or bedrock, water already present, and soil temperature.
Warm soils take in water faster, while frozen soils such as permafrost may not absorb it at all, depending on how they froze.
The Richards equation gives the rate of change of moisture in unsaturated soil; first published by Lewis Richardson in 1922, it is solved numerically by software such as Hydrus.
The lab manual puts saturated flow at tensions of 0 to -0.3 bar, driven by hydrostatic head, and unsaturated flow at 0.3 to 31 bars, driven by a tension gradient.

title: Preferential flow

definition.text: Rapid drainage of water under gravity along connected macropores, crevices, and root and worm channels in soil.

facts.text: Macropores and fractures strongly influence infiltration rates in many soils, along with preferential flow patterns and hydraulic conductivity.
Living or dead tree roots open preferential channels for rainwater that can raise infiltration rates up to 27 times.
Preferential paths speed drainage, but they also carry dissolved nutrients away quickly and leave water and chemicals unevenly spread in the soil.
Extreme forms in depressions speed the transport of contaminants toward groundwater.
Water that cannot enter strongly water-repellent patches finds preferential pathways that take it deeper into the profile.
Soil mixing by organisms and other disturbances creates preferential paths for soil gas and infiltrating water.
In soils with distinct macropores, preferential flow dominates measurements made with single- or double-ring infiltrometers under ponding.
Soil physics models often add preferential flow as dual-porosity or dual-permeability options, but these are generally bolted onto the Richards solution without rigorous physical grounding.

title: Fingered flow

definition.text: Uneven downward flow of water through unsaturated soil in narrow 'gravity fingers'.

facts.text: Soil moisture sources attribute gravity fingers to surface tension between water particles.
Fingering in the unsaturated zone is described as a Saffman–Taylor instability, arising mostly during drainage and leaving an unstable boundary between saturated and unsaturated soil.

notes: No article of its own; mentioned on Soil moisture and Water content. The two pages name different causes (surface tension; Saffman–Taylor instability) without calling it a dispute.

title: Percolation

definition.text: The downward drainage of water through a soil after the soil has absorbed it.

facts.text: Water that drains through macropores under gravity when it rains is called gravitational water; drainage stops at field capacity, when adhesion and cohesion hold the rest.
Once a soil is fully wetted, extra water percolates below the roots, carrying clay, humus, nutrients (mostly cations) and contaminants that may pollute groundwater.
Magnesium, sulfur and potassium leach most readily, nitrogen little unless nitrate fertilizer was recently applied, and phosphorus very little.
Deep percolation that reaches groundwater is groundwater recharge, and groundwater in turn feeds soil moisture through percolation.

notes: No article of its own (Percolation not crawled); passes the mentioned-on-two-or-more-pages test (Soil water (retention), Soil moisture, Groundwater, Groundwater recharge, Eluvium).

definition.text: The ways plants draw soil water into their roots, mainly by the pull of transpiration and partly by osmosis.

facts.text: Most soil water enters plants passively, pulled up the column of xylem sap from roots to leaves as water transpires, as the cohesion-tension theory describes.
Salts concentrated in roots create an osmotic gradient that pushes water in; osmotic uptake matters most when transpiration is low, at night or in high humidity.
The root endodermis and leaf stomata regulate the upward flow, which cavitation in the xylem can interrupt.
A winter rye plant grown four months in 0.0283 cubic metres of loam formed 620 km of roots and 10,620 km of root hairs, yet touched only 1.2% of the soil volume.
Because roots grow into new soil every day, the volume they explore, and the water they take up, grows greatly over a season.
Root architecture, the spatial layout of the root system, helps plants adapt to the soil's water and nutrient supply.
Grain sorghum held at 1300 kPa soil suction from seed-head emergence to seed set lost 34% of its production.
Some parts of a root system can also re-wet dry parts of the soil.

title: Evapotranspiration

definition.text: The combined movement of water from the Earth's surface, open water, ice, bare soil and plants, into the atmosphere by evaporation and transpiration.

facts.text: Evaporation moves water straight to the air from soil and water bodies; transpiration carries it from roots through the plant and out of the stomata as vapour.
Only 0.1% to 1% of the water a plant uses stays in it; most is lost through transpiration.
It is measured as millimetres of water over a set time, and returns on average three-fifths to three-quarters of land precipitation to the atmosphere.
It is controlled mainly by the water available in soil and water bodies, the energy in air and soil, and the atmosphere's capacity to take up moisture.
Drier soil means less evapotranspiration and a warmer soil surface; where potential evapotranspiration exceeds rainfall, soil dries out unless irrigated.
It is measured directly with a weighing lysimeter, or estimated from a catchment water balance, an energy balance or meteorological data.
Evapotranspiration is one of four main parts of the water balance at a point, with infiltration, deep leakage beyond roots and surface runoff.
Evapotranspiration can concentrate the salts in irrigation water to toxic levels.

title: Transpiration ratio
article: Soil moisture#Consumptive use and water use efficiency

definition.text: A measure of water use efficiency: the water a plant transpires divided by the dry weight of the harvested plant.

facts.text: Transpiration ratios for crops range from 300 to 700.
Alfalfa may have a ratio of 500, so 500 kilograms of water produce one kilogram of dry alfalfa.

definition.text: Soil suction is the negative of soil water potential, the force needed to pull water out of soil; pF is the common logarithm of suction in centimetres of water.

facts.text: Water stays in soil where its adhesion to the oxygen of soil particles beats the cohesion between water molecules, and the strength of that hold sets its availability to plants.
Suction is given in kPa, bar (100 kPa) or cm of water (about 0.098 kPa); pF 3 equals 1000 cm, 98 kPa or 0.98 bar.
As roots thin a water film, adhesion raises suction up to 1500 kPa (pF 4.2), the wilting point.
Air-dry soil is at 100,000 kPa suction (pF 6) and oven-dry soil at 1,000,000 kPa (pF 7).

title: Water content

definition.text: The quantity of water contained in a material such as soil, where it is called soil moisture.

facts.text: It is a ratio, from 0 when completely dry up to the material's porosity at saturation.
It can be given by volume (volumetric water content, θ) or by mass (gravimetric water content).
Soil science, like geotechnics, gives gravimetric water content relative to the sample's dry weight; multiplying it by the bulk specific gravity converts it to volumetric content.
In saturated aquifers volumetric water content equals porosity; most soils hold less than their porosity, which defines unsaturated conditions, the subject of vadose zone hydrogeology.
Depending on its water content, soil is solid, semi-solid, plastic or liquid; the water contents where it changes state are the Atterberg limits.
Water content matters for groundwater recharge, agriculture and soil chemistry.
Spatial variance in water content tends to rise with overall wetness in semiarid regions, fall with it in humid regions and peak at intermediate wetness in temperate regions.

title: Standard soil water contents

definition.text: Four reference water contents routinely measured in soil science, saturation, field capacity, permanent wilting point and residual water, each tied to a suction.

facts.text: Saturated water content, θs, is at 0 kPa suction and typically 0.2–0.5 by volume, equivalent to effective porosity.
Field capacity, θfc, is at −33 kPa and typically 0.1–0.35, the moisture 2–3 days after rain or irrigation.
Permanent wilting point, θpwp, is at −1500 kPa and typically 0.01–0.25, the lowest moisture at which a plant wilts.
Residual water content, θr, is the water left at very high tension, typically 0.001–0.1.
Available water content is field capacity minus wilting point, ranging from 0.1 in gravel to 0.3 in peat.
Average values put sand's wilting point at 3.3% and field capacity at 9.1% by volume, against 27.2% and 39.6% for clay.
Available water peaks in silt loam at 19.7% by volume, against 5.8% in sand and 12.4% in clay.

title: Degree of saturation

definition.text: A measure, used in soil mechanics and petroleum engineering, of how fully a material's pore space is filled with water.

facts.text: It runs from 0 when dry to 1 when saturated, but real materials never reach either value; both are idealizations for engineering.
Normalized water content, or effective saturation, is a dimensionless value defined by van Genuchten from the residual and saturated water contents.
Residual water content is where the slope of water content against suction head becomes zero; saturated water content equals porosity.

notes: S:3bd5f56c84b4 carries CLARIFICATION NEEDED; the defining formula itself is not in the sentence text.

definition.text: The direct measurement of water content by drying a sample in an oven and comparing its weight before and after.

facts.text: The sample is dried in a special oven or kiln and weighed at regular intervals until drying is complete.
The mass lost is the water; dividing it by the wet or the dry mass, depending on the discipline, gives gravimetric water content.
Volumetric water content also needs the sample's total volume, fixed by filling a container of known volume, such as a tin can, when sampling.
Because this needs a sample removed, dried and weighed, soil moisture sensors estimate water content indirectly from electrical resistance, dielectric constant or neutron interaction.

definition.text: Estimating soil water content in place, with probes in the soil or by remote sensing, instead of drying samples.

facts.text: Several geophysical methods approximate water content in situ, including time-domain reflectometry, neutron probes, frequency domain sensors, capacitance probes, amplitude domain reflectometry, electrical resistivity tomography and ground-penetrating radar.
Geophysical sensors often monitor soil moisture continuously for agriculture and research.
Estimates range in scale from sensors in the soil to satellite imagery combined with hydrological models.
Each method has pros and cons, so combining techniques can reduce the drawbacks of any one.
Some farmers now schedule irrigation from soil moisture measurements, a practice called smart irrigation.

definition.text: Estimating surface soil moisture from satellites with microwaves, using the large contrast in dielectric properties between wet and dry soil.

facts.text: Microwaves are insensitive to atmospheric conditions, pass through clouds, and partly penetrate vegetation to read the ground surface.
Satellites used include WindSat, AMSR-E, RADARSAT, ERS-1-2, Metop/ASCAT and SMAP.

title: Neutron probe

definition.text: A device that measures the quantity of water in soil.

facts.text: A pellet of americium-241 and beryllium produces fast neutrons when alpha particles from the americium strike the beryllium nuclei.
The neutrons slow down on hitting hydrogen nuclei in the soil; counting the slow neutrons that return estimates the hydrogen, and so the water, present.
Read through an access tube installed in the soil, it is used in agriculture for highly accurate deep-soil readings.
Neutron probes can gauge soil water potential over a range of 0 to −1500 kPa.

title: Agricultural drought

definition.text: A condition in which soil is too dry to sustain reliable plant growth.

facts.text: It is a particular focus of irrigation management and common in arid and semi-arid environments.
As soil dries, transpiration falls because water is held ever more tightly by suction; below the wilting point plants wilt and stop transpiring.
Agricultural or ecological droughts harm crop production or ecosystems generally.
It can arise without any fall in rainfall, when more irrigation, or soil conditions and erosion from poorly planned farming, leave crops short of water.

notes: No article of its own; mentioned on Water content and Drought (§ Categories).

title: Water potential

definition.text: The potential energy of water per unit volume, compared with pure water under reference conditions.

facts.text: It expresses water's tendency to move from place to place because of osmosis, gravity, mechanical pressure and matrix effects such as capillary action.
Unrestricted water moves from higher to lower water potential; dissolved solutes lower the potential and added pressure raises it.
It is usually given as energy per unit volume and written with the Greek letter ψ; in soils the reference is usually pure water at the soil surface.
In soil, total water potential is the sum of matric potential from capillary action, osmotic potential in saline soil and gravitational potential for downward flow.
Soil sits at 0 kPa when saturated, −33 kPa at field capacity and −1500 kPa at the permanent wilting point; dry air is typically about −100 MPa.
Water flows passively from soil to roots, up the stem, to the leaves and into the air because each step has a more negative potential than the one before.
Tensiometers measure 0 to −85 kPa, electrical resistance blocks −90 to −1500 kPa, neutron probes 0 to −1500 kPa, and TDR 0 to −10,000 kPa.

notes: The Water potential lead sentence S:e413c2092dea has a sapling sentence run into it; not cited for that part.

definition.text: The part of water potential that comes from water's attraction to solid particles, such as clay or sand in soil, and the menisci it forms between them.

facts.text: Adhesion to solids, together with cohesion among water molecules, creates surface tension and menisci in the soil matrix, and force is needed to break them.
Its size depends on the spacing between particles, which sets meniscus width, and on the chemistry of the solid matrix.
It is always negative, since water held by the matrix has less energy than pure water, and it occurs only in unsaturated soil above the water table.
Near zero, nearly all pores are full and the soil holds its maximum; water draining into less moist soil of similar porosity is generally at −10 to −30 kPa.
It is often large compared with the other components, and though the flow it drives may be slow, it is vital for supplying water to roots.

definition.text: The part of water potential lowered by dissolved solutes; with pure water set at zero, it can never be positive.

facts.text: Soil solution has an osmotic potential from its inorganic and organic solutes, and the more solute, the lower it is.
Because zones of soil are rarely separated by a semipermeable membrane, osmotic potential has little effect on the mass movement of water in soil.
It strongly affects plants: in soils high in soluble salts, the soil solution's lower osmotic potential severely restricts water uptake by roots.
In salty soils it can fall so low that the cells of young seedlings collapse by plasmolysis.

definition.text: The relationship between a soil's water content and its soil water potential.

facts.text: Also called the soil moisture characteristic, it differs between soil types and is used to predict water storage, plant water supply and aggregate stability.
Near zero potential the soil is almost saturated and holds water mainly by capillarity; as it dries, water is bound ever more strongly in the smallest pores, at grain contacts and as adsorbed films.
Sandy soils, held mainly by capillarity, release most of their water at higher potentials; clayey soils, with adhesive and osmotic binding, release it at lower ones.
At any given potential, peaty soils usually hold far more water than clayey soils, which hold more than sandy soils.
A soil's water-holding capacity comes from its porosity and the nature of the bonding within it.
Because pores fill and drain differently, hysteresis gives separate wetting and drying curves.
Edgar Buckingham made the first water retention curve in 1907, for six soils from sand to clay, from soil columns 48 inches tall.

definition.text: An equation that describes the shape of a soil's water retention curve.

facts.text: Its parameter α relates to the inverse of the air-entry suction, and n, greater than 1, measures the pore-size distribution.
Its parameterization led to a model predicting how unsaturated hydraulic conductivity varies with saturation and pressure.
α and n come from field or laboratory tests such as the instantaneous profile method, fitted by non-linear least squares; Gaussian process regression on the residuals can improve the fit.
Alternative retention models include Brooks–Corey, Broadbridge–White and Rogers–Stallybrass–Clements.

title: Field capacity

definition.text: The water a soil still holds after excess water has drained away and downward movement has slowed.

facts.text: It is usually reached two to three days after rain or irrigation in pervious soils of uniform structure and texture.
By convention it is the water content held at −33 kPa (−0.33 bar) of suction, or −10 kPa for sandy soils, after work by Richards and Weaver.
At field capacity the smallest pores hold water and the largest hold air, the optimal condition for plant growth and microbial activity.
The water held depends on the specific surface area of the particles, so clay-rich and organic soils have higher field capacities.
It is measured by wetting a profile, covering it against evaporation and tracking water content; the point where macropore drainage stops is also called the drained upper limit.
The term came from Israelsen and West and from Veihmeyer and Hendrickson, improving on Lyman Briggs's moisture equivalent.
Veihmeyer and Hendrickson admitted it is not strictly a constant for a soil, but a practical measure of water-holding capacity.
Groundwater recharge is most likely when the water reaching a soil exceeds its field capacity.

notes: S:925fad7d4126 (DATED) says Veihmeyer and Hendrickson proposed the concept in 1949, yet S:dd87b0302b0c, on the term's origin, cites 1931 and 1922; the verification pass should check the date.

definition.text: The lowest amount of soil water a plant needs in order not to wilt.

facts.text: At or below it a plant wilts and cannot regain turgor even when kept in a saturated atmosphere for 12 hours.
By convention it is the water content at −1,500 kPa (−15 bar) of suction, as Lorenzo A. Richards proposed.
It roughly marks the boundary between available and unavailable water; there seeds will not germinate, and plants wilt and die unless adapted to recover.
Closing stomata can slow transpiration and delay wilting below the wilting point, especially in plants adapted to drought.
In 1912 Briggs and Shantz proposed the wilting coefficient, the water content at which plants first wilt beyond recovery without added water.
Veihmeyer and Hendrickson of UC Davis found it to be a constant of the soil, independent of environmental conditions.
Experiments by Richards and colleagues fixed today's accepted limits for plant growth: −1/3 bar at field capacity and −15 bar at the permanent wilting point.

title: Capillary fringe

definition.text: The layer just above a water table into which groundwater rises by capillary action to fill the pores.

facts.text: Its base is saturated by tension, but this saturated part is shorter than the total capillary rise because pore sizes are mixed.
Small, uniform pores can keep soil saturated several feet above the water table, while large pores limit the saturated part to a few inches.
Above the saturated base, water content falls with height above the water table.
Definitions differ: solute-transport workers count only the tension-saturated base, while salinity, vapor-phase and bioremediation workers include the unsaturated part too.
Land whose surface lies within the capillary fringe of saline groundwater salinizes rapidly.
Where the water table meets soil it forms an oxic–anoxic zone, and oxygen from it feeds microbes that break down dissolved organic compounds.

notes: Workers define the fringe differently (S:e86f9328e768, S:5a365e83c838, S:1b0fa3f56439); a difference of convention, not a dispute.

definition.text: The process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil.

facts.text: It is driven by gravity, capillary forces, absorption and osmosis, and many soil characteristics affect its rate.
Infiltration capacity is the maximum rate, usually given in metres per day; it falls as the surface layers get wetter.
When rain arrives faster than the soil can take it in, runoff usually follows unless a physical barrier holds the water.
Infiltration continues only while there is room at the surface, which depends on porosity and on how fast earlier water moves down.
Robert E. Horton suggested that capacity drops quickly early in a storm, then settles to a near-constant value after a couple of hours.
Infiltrated water fills storage and weakens capillary pull, wetted clays swell and narrow pores, and raindrops on bare ground wash fine particles into surface pores.
Rates range from 0.25 cm per hour in high-clay soils to 2.5 cm per hour in sand and well-aggregated soils.
Infiltrometers, permeameters and rainfall simulators all measure infiltration rates.

definition.text: The rainfall, soil and surface conditions that control how fast water enters a soil.

facts.text: Rain infiltrates faster than snow or sleet; infiltration is rapid at the start of a storm, while soil is unsaturated, and slows as it saturates.
Fine-pored clays take water more slowly than coarse sands, except dry clays, which crack and take it quickly.
Compaction lowers porosity and so infiltration capacity, and hydrophobic soils after wildfires can cut infiltration sharply or stop it.
Dry soils have the highest capacity, partly saturated soils a moderate rate, and saturated soils no room for more.
Roots and burrowing animals open cracks that speed infiltration; with no vegetation rates can be very low, causing excess runoff and erosion.
On sandy loam, infiltration under litter can be nine times that of bare ground, where a soil crust or surface seal keeps it low.
Pavement and other impermeable surfaces prevent infiltration and increase runoff, and steeper slopes shed water faster.
Alkali soils have poor structure and low infiltration capacity, so rainwater ponds and evaporates before crops can use it.

definition.text: Methods for estimating the volume and rate of water infiltrating a soil.

facts.text: Infiltration is one term of the general hydrologic budget; if every other term is known, simple algebra gives it.
The rigorous standard, coupling groundwater and surface water through non-uniform soil, is the numerical solution of Richards' equation.
Richards' equation is computationally expensive, not guaranteed to converge, and sometimes struggles to conserve mass.
The finite water-content vadose zone flow method approximates it as three ordinary differential equations that always converge and conserve mass, assuming vertical flow and uniform layers.
For uniform initial water content in deep, well-drained soil, good approximate methods give the infiltration flux for a single rain event.
A simplified Darcy's law method assumes the gradient acts over an arbitrary length and omits cumulative depth, and many argue it is too simple to use.

title: Green–Ampt method

definition.text: An infiltration model, named after Green and Ampt, that estimates infiltration from soil suction head, porosity, hydraulic conductivity and time.

facts.text: It accounts for more variables than methods such as the simplified Darcy's law approach.
It gives cumulative infiltration depth F(t) through F(t) = Kt + ψΔθ ln[1 + F(t)/ψΔθ], solved iteratively since F appears on both sides.
It assumes the depth of ponded water above the surface is negligible.

notes: The formula in S:126641ad4d2b is printed as 'ln⁡[1+F(t)ψΔθ]' (fraction lost in extraction); the fact restores the division.

definition.text: An empirical formula, named after Robert E. Horton, in which infiltration starts at an initial rate and declines exponentially with time.

facts.text: Once soil saturation reaches a certain level, the rate levels off at a constant equilibrium rate, fc, the minimum infiltration rate.
Integrated, it gives the total volume infiltrated after a given time.
It matches Horton's observation that infiltration capacity falls quickly early in a storm and then tends to a near-constant value.

definition.text: An empirical infiltration equation that assumes the intake rate declines over time as a power function.

facts.text: Its main limitation is that it implies a final intake rate of zero, whereas infiltration usually approaches a finite steady value.
The Kostiakov–Lewis, or modified Kostiakov, equation fixes this by adding a steady intake term.

title: Sorptivity

definition.text: A measure of a porous medium's capacity to absorb or release liquid by capillarity, a term introduced by John Philip in 1957.

facts.text: It is widely used to characterize soils and porous building materials such as brick, stone and concrete.
Philip showed in 1969 that sorptivity can be found from horizontal infiltration, where flow is mostly capillary absorption, by relating cumulative infiltration to time.
Its SI unit is m·s−1/2; for vertical infiltration Philip's solution adds a second parameter, giving equations valid for short times.
Clapp and Hornberger derived average sorptivity values, with retention and saturated conductivity parameters, for different texture classes.

definition.text: A device that measures the rate at which water infiltrates soil or another porous medium.

facts.text: Common types are single-ring and double-ring infiltrometers, disc permeameters and falling-head infiltrometers.
A single ring is driven into the soil and fed at constant head, often from a Mariotte's bottle, or at falling head while the operator records how much water enters.
Holding a constant head makes the supply rate equal the infiltration capacity, and the rate of entry relates to the soil's hydraulic conductivity.
Driving the ring in deforms the soil, rings cannot reliably represent furrow, sprinkler or rain infiltration, and a single ring lets water spread sideways.
Ring infiltrometers measure only ponded, saturated flow, which preferential flow dominates in soils with distinct macropores.

definition.text: An infiltrometer with an inner ring and a larger outer ring around it, which keeps the flow from the inner ring one-dimensional.

facts.text: Water is supplied at constant or falling head, and the operator records how much enters the soil from the inner ring over a set time.
With steady one-dimensional flow and a unit gradient below, the infiltration rate approximately equals the saturated hydraulic conductivity.
The ASTM standard method uses inner and outer rings of 30 and 60 cm diameter.

definition.text: In soil, a cavity larger than 75 μm.

facts.text: Macropores carry preferential flow and fast transport of solutes and colloids, raising hydraulic conductivity so water infiltrates and drains quickly.
They lie between peds and between large sand or gravel grains, and are made by cracks, plant roots and soil fauna.
Wet–dry and freeze–thaw cycles crack soil into macropores; those made by roots and organisms such as earthworms are called biopores.
Macropore formation generally decreases with depth, as the processes behind it weaken.
Water moves freely under gravity in macropores but is held by capillarity in micropores; at field capacity macropores are generally air-filled.
They aid infiltration, groundwater recharge and gas exchange with the air, but can also wash nitrate from nitrogen fertilizers into groundwater.
Tillage and compaction easily alter them; compacted forest landings have little macroporosity, and added organic matter can improve it.
Colloid and surface chemists define macropores in porous solids differently, as cavities larger than 50 nm.

definition.text: The linked system of a soil's macropores, irregular in shape, size and roughness, whose geometry shapes water movement, aeration and root growth.

facts.text: Higher connectivity usually means higher permeability, and links to the surface and to groundwater aid infiltration and recharge.
Connected pores may still not be continuous; dead-end pores block or slow water and air, while continuous pores improve aeration and room for roots.
Tortuosity, the ratio of actual path length to the straight distance between two points, measures resistance to flow: the more sinuous the path, the higher it is.

title: Permeability (porous media)

definition.text: A measure of how readily a fluid, gas or liquid, flows through a porous material such as rock or soil, usually written k.

facts.text: It depends on porosity, but also on the shapes of the pores and how well they connect, and on the pressure inside the material.
Its SI unit is the square metre; the practical unit is the darcy or millidarcy, with 1 darcy about 10−12 m², named after the engineer Henry Darcy.
Most materials range from a fraction to several thousand millidarcys; unconsolidated sands may exceed 5000 millidarcys.
Intrinsic permeability belongs to the solid skeleton and microstructure alone, whatever the fluid; hydraulic conductivity is the overall constant for water flow, of which it is a part.
Keeping the two apart lets temperature effects on viscosity, and fluids other than water such as brines or petroleum, be taken into account.
It is usually measured in the lab with Darcy's law under steady flow, or estimated from empirical formulas; for simple models such as packed identical spheres it can be calculated.
It matters for groundwater in aquifers, oil and gas reservoirs, filtration, and deciding whether ground suits construction.
Natural values span many orders of magnitude, from well-sorted gravel among the most pervious materials to unweathered clay and fresh granite among the least.

notes: § Absolute permeability sentence S:8a34e0b999af carries CLARIFICATION NEEDED; not cited.

title: Permeability of soils

definition.text: A soil's capacity to let water pass, which depends on particle size, impurities in the water, void ratio, degree of saturation, adsorbed water, entrapped air and organic material.

facts.text: Allen Hazen found a soil's coefficient of permeability proportional to the square of its particle size, so coarse sand may be over a million times more permeable than clay.
Fine particulate impurities progressively clog the pores and lower permeability.
Permeability rises with void ratio; whatever the exact relation, every soil gives a straight line when void ratio is plotted against log k.
Air pockets in partly saturated soil block water, so its permeability is much lower than when saturated, and Darcy's law does not strictly apply.
Fine-grained soils carry a strongly attached layer of adsorbed water that cannot move under gravity and obstructs flow through the pores.
Entrapped air and organic matter cut permeability considerably, so samples for permeability tests should be fully saturated.
Compaction reduces a soil's permeability to water and so increases runoff, while vegetative cover raises it.

notes: The page's Background and Composition sections (S:79beb8c61569 to S:dea782f6ae59) describe soil aeration and soil air, not permeability; left to Soil aeration. The void-ratio relation in S:28488b3a6d43 is garbled ('e/sup>/(1+e)') and S:39cbac81a912 gives e² or e³/(1+e); not cited.

definition.text: A property of soils, rocks and other porous materials that describes how easily a fluid, usually water, moves through their pores or fractures; written K, in metres per second.

facts.text: It depends on the material's intrinsic permeability, its degree of saturation, and the density and viscosity of the fluid.
It is the ratio of volume flux to hydraulic gradient; saturated hydraulic conductivity, Ksat, describes flow through saturated material.
Sand and gravel aquifers, with high porosity and permeability, conduct water far better than clay or unfractured granite, so wells draw water from them more easily.
Natural values span many orders of magnitude, often lognormally, vary greatly in space, and depend on direction: vertical K can be orders of magnitude below horizontal K.
K depends on scale: testing a cubic metre of aquifer generally gives a different result from a cubic centimetre sample.
Unsaturated K depends non-linearly on water content, and one material's unsaturated K spans a wider range than saturated K across all materials.
It is found empirically, from pore-size and grain-size distributions and texture, or experimentally, from laboratory and field tests interpreted with Darcy's law.
It has dimensions of length per time, such as m/s or ft/day.

title: Hazen's formula

definition.text: Allen Hazen's empirical formula for approximating hydraulic conductivity from a grain-size analysis.

facts.text: It uses D10, the diameter at the 10th percentile of grain size, and an empirical coefficient C between 0.0 and 1.5 depending on the source, averaging 1.0.
Behind it lies Hazen's finding that a soil's coefficient of permeability is proportional to the square of particle size.
Laboratory pumping tests have been used to check such formulas for sandy soils, and some studies found a modified Hazen formula approximates laboratory measurements reasonably well.

notes: S:a9975d47135d (C usually 1.0 to 1.5, D in mm, K in cm/s) carries CITATION NEEDED; not cited.

definition.text: A simple, inexpensive laboratory test of hydraulic conductivity in which water flows through a soil specimen under a steady head.

facts.text: It is typically used on granular soil.
The volume of water passing in a set time is measured, and K follows by rearranging Darcy's law with the specimen's length, cross-section and head.
The head defines an excess mass of water whose weight sets the pressure difference across the sample, ρgh.

definition.text: A laboratory test of hydraulic conductivity in which a saturated soil sample drains with no water added, so the head declines over time.

facts.text: Unlike the constant-head method, it works for both fine-grained and coarse-grained soils.
K is calculated from how far the head drops in a given time.

definition.text: Measurements of hydraulic conductivity made in place in the field rather than on samples in a laboratory.

facts.text: Field methods give the most reliable values with the least disturbance, since disturbance of laboratory samples undermines their results.
Small-scale tests watch water levels in cavities: infiltration tests above the water table and slug tests below it.
Large-scale tests include pumping tests in wells and observing how existing horizontal drainage systems perform.
The pumping test, in pumping-in and pumping-out forms, is called the most reliable way to find a soil's coefficient of permeability.

definition.text: A slug test that measures hydraulic conductivity below a shallow water table from the rate at which water refills an auger hole.

facts.text: A hole is augered to below the water table, water is bailed out, and the rate at which the level rises again is recorded.
It gives the horizontal saturated hydraulic conductivity in metres per day.
Hooghoudt developed it in the Netherlands in 1934, and Van Bavel and Kirkham introduced it to the US in 1948.
Measurements across 100 ha varied by a factor of 25, with a lognormal distribution.

definition.text: A measure of how much water a soil layer or aquifer can transmit horizontally, as toward a pumping well.

facts.text: A layer's transmissivity is proportional to its horizontal hydraulic conductivity and saturated thickness; in m/day and m it comes out in m²/day.
An aquifer's total transmissivity is the sum of its layers', and it can be found from pumping tests.
Layers above the water table are unsaturated and add nothing, so transmissivity changes as the water table moves; drawdown in an unconfined aquifer reduces flow to a well.

definition.text: The condition of a soil layer or aquifer whose horizontal and vertical hydraulic conductivity differ considerably.

facts.text: In layered aquifers, horizontal flow runs mainly through layers of high horizontal permeability, while low-permeability layers pass water mainly vertically; a layer's vertical resistance is expressed in days.
An aquifer is semi-confined when a poorly conducting aquitard overlies a highly conducting layer, so flow is mainly vertical in the first and horizontal in the second.
Flow to drains or wells for water-table control must allow for anisotropy, or the result may be wrong.
In anisotropic media permeability becomes a symmetric, positive-definite 3 by 3 tensor whose eigenvectors give the principal flow directions.

title: Darcy's law

definition.text: An equation that describes the flow of a fluid through a porous medium.

facts.text: Henry Darcy formulated it from experiments on water flowing through beds of sand, and it became the basis of hydrogeology.
From the 1830s Darcy studied flow through sand filters to improve the water supply of Dijon, France, and published the law in an 1856 construction report.
Like Ohm's law, it relates flow rate linearly to the difference in hydraulic head through the hydraulic conductivity, which plays the part of electrical conductivity.
Flow rate rises with the medium's permeability, cross-section and pressure drop, and falls with the fluid's viscosity and the length of the flow path.
The Darcy flux is a flow rate per unit area, not the speed of water in the pores; porosity links the two.
Without a pressure gradient nothing flows; with one, flow runs from high to low pressure, grows with the gradient, and differs between materials under the same gradient.
It holds only for slow, viscous, laminar flow, as in most groundwater: Reynolds numbers below one, and up to 10 in tests; very coarse sediments may flow turbulently.
It is a special case of the Stokes equation, derived from the Navier–Stokes equations, and parallels Fourier's law of heat conduction and Fick's law of diffusion.

notes: Petroleum-engineering sections (multiphase flow after Muskat, 1936; Klinkenberg correction; Brinkman form; short-time-scale form) left out as outside soil science.

definition.text: An extension of Darcy's law that adds an inertial term for fast flow through porous media, where flow no longer varies linearly with pressure.

facts.text: Above Reynolds numbers of about 1 to 10, inertial effects become significant and Darcy's law no longer holds.
The extra term uses an inertial permeability, measured in metres.
The departure comes from changes in the shape of flow streamlines at the pore scale, induced by recirculation zones.
Flow within a sandstone reservoir is usually too slow to need it, but gas flow into a production well or through rough fractures may justify it.

title: Darcy (unit)

definition.text: A unit of permeability, with the millidarcy as its thousandth, named after Henry Darcy.

facts.text: A medium of 1 darcy lets 1 cm³/s of a fluid with viscosity 1 cP pass through 1 cm² under a pressure gradient of 1 atm/cm.
1 darcy equals 9.869233×10−13 m², usually approximated as 1 μm².
Values run from as high as 100,000 darcys for gravel to under 0.01 microdarcys for granite; sand is about 1 darcy.
Not an SI unit, it is widely used in petroleum engineering and geology; in hydrology, 1 darcy corresponds to a water flux of 0.831 m/day under hydrostatic pressure at 20 °C.

notes: Sand is 'approximately 1 darcy' here (S:f6ed47db3688) while Permeability (porous media) says unconsolidated sands may exceed 5000 md (S:f80fa4ed231b); a typical value against a range, flagged for the verification pass rather than as a conflict.

definition.text: A field instrument that measures water infiltration into soil under tension, giving in situ saturated and unsaturated hydraulic properties.

facts.text: It is used mainly to estimate hydraulic conductivity near saturation; in the US it is called the tension infiltrometer.
Ring infiltrometers measure only ponded flow, which macropores dominate where present, so a negative potential is applied to exclude macropores and measure flow through the soil matrix alone.
Perroux and White of CSIRO developed it in 1988, building on designs such as the Gardners' 1939 negative-head permeameter and Clothier and White's 1981 sorptivity tube.
A nylon mesh membrane, a water reservoir and a bubbling tower supply potentials from −200 mm to 0 mm, excluding pores wider than 0.075 mm.

title: Pedotransfer function

definition.text: A predictive function that estimates soil properties from soil survey data.

facts.text: Johan Bouma coined the term in 1989 for 'translating data we have into what we need', though the idea had long been applied.
PTFs turn readily available survey data, such as field morphology, texture, structure and pH, into estimates of properties that are laborious and costly to measure.
They are empirical methods, used mainly in soil science and increasingly in hydrogeology, built with regression and data-mining techniques.
Most research has targeted the water retention curve and hydraulic conductivity, which are hard and costly to measure and have large databases.
The first PTF, by Briggs and McLane in 1907, gave the wilting coefficient as 0.01 sand + 0.12 silt + 0.57 clay.
In the 1960s Salter and Williams related texture classes and particle-size distribution to available water capacity, giving what are now called class and continuous PTFs.
PTFs also estimate physical, mechanical, chemical and biological properties, and programs such as the USDA's ROSETTA use neural networks to apply them.
In soil inference systems such as SINFERS, introduced by McBratney and colleagues in 2002, linked PTFs act as the knowledge rules.

notes: Dates to verify: S:176c6ea1ff9a credits field capacity and wilting point to Veihmeyer and Hendrickson (1927), while Field capacity S:925fad7d4126 says 1949; Briggs and McLane (1907) determined the wilting coefficient here, while Permanent wilting point S:da07fb8f9841 has Briggs and Shantz propose it in 1912.

definition.text: An equation for the speed at which water moves down through unsaturated soil under the combined pull of gravity and capillarity.

facts.text: It is a reworking of Richards' equation in which the unknown is the depth of a wetting front of a given water content as it moves with time.
Its advection-like term carries flow driven by gravity and the capillarity of the wetting front; its diffusion-like term, much like Fick's second law, reflects the shape of the front.
Dropping the diffusion-like term still gave over 99% accuracy in cumulative infiltration when checked against exact solutions of Richards' equation for idealized soils.
Solved by the method of lines, the advection-like term becomes three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater.

title: Soil moisture zone

definition.text: The depth of soil from which plant roots draw water, often called the root zone.

facts.text: Water that moves below the root zone after heavy rain or irrigation is lost to plants and can take fertilizers and nutrients with it.
Irrigation scheduling aims to wet the whole root zone while keeping overwatering to a minimum.
Salts that build up in the root zone can be carried deeper, or into groundwater, by recharge.

notes: The article is a one-sentence stub (S:b6352a367ac2); facts come from root-zone sentences on Hydrophobic soil, Irrigation scheduling and Groundwater recharge.

definition.text: The unbroken pathway along which water moves from the soil, through plants, into the atmosphere.

facts.text: Water potential is very low in the air and higher inside leaves, so water diffuses out through the stomata as vapour.
Water evaporating from leaf cells is replaced from the xylem, where cohesion and tension pull more water up from the roots.
Each discipline describes its own segment differently: soil physics by tension, physiology by diffusion pressure deficit, meteorology by vapour pressure or humidity.
The concept treats soil, plants, animals and air as one dynamic system, giving water in each part a water potential, which is the basis for modelling transport between them.

definition.text: An emerging field joining soil science and hydrology that studies the interface between the pedosphere and the hydrosphere.

facts.text: Like hydrogeology, hydroclimatology and ecohydrology, it links hydrology with another of the Earth's spheres.
Soil hydrology and hydropedology are listed among the areas of practice of soil science.
The biomantle shows such roles: loosened by bioturbation, it speeds percolation through biopores and carries downslope throughflow above dense subsoil horizons.

title: Groundwater recharge

definition.text: The downward movement of water from the surface to groundwater, also called deep drainage or deep percolation.

facts.text: Fed mainly by rain and snowmelt, and less by rivers and lakes, recharge is the main way water enters an aquifer.
It usually takes place in the vadose zone below plant roots and is often expressed as a flux to the water table.
Diffuse recharge is rain soaking through soil over large areas; focused recharge leaks from rivers, lakes, wetlands or depressions and grows more dominant as aridity increases.
Paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, reduce infiltration, increase runoff and so cut recharge.
Yet urban recharge can be up to ten times higher than rural, because leaking water-supply and sewage networks add water that rural areas lack.
For sustainable use, long-term abstraction from an aquifer should not exceed the rate at which it is recharged.
Recharge can flush salts that accumulate in the root zone into deeper layers or into groundwater.
Under climate change, fewer but more intense storms may raise recharge in many places, while harsher droughts may dry and compact soils and reduce infiltration.

notes: The page says paving and development impede recharge (S:5a4e55ded96d) and also that urbanization raises it via leaking supply and sewer networks while reducing infiltration (S:5776e0b65a3b, S:006beedf456d); different mechanisms, not a value conflict.

definition.text: Recharge in which rain falling fairly evenly over an area reaches groundwater mainly beneath surface depressions where runoff gathers.

facts.text: Rain spread evenly within the soil's field capacity barely percolates; pooled in low spots, the same volume can exceed field capacity and drain down to groundwater.
Water tables rise beneath such depressions, and the process can be very important in arid regions.
Deeper ponding forces water in faster, dislodging adsorbed contaminants and carrying them to the water table, so the quality of water in infiltration basins is a special concern.
In karst, focused flow can dissolve tunnels down to aquifers, an extreme form of preferential flow that speeds contaminant transport.

definition.text: Recharge engineered by people, routing rainwater or reclaimed water into the subsurface.

facts.text: Managed aquifer recharge methods include modifying streambed channels, bank filtration, water spreading and recharge wells.
A facility in Orange County, California, cleans and injects 100 million gallons per day, or 90 billion gallons per year.
In India, where farmers' over-pumping has depleted groundwater, the government in 2007 funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts of seven states.
Stormwater pollution collects in retention basins, and high water tables affect how detention ponds, retention ponds and rain gardens should be designed.

definition.text: The methods used to estimate how much water reaches the water table, which no widely applicable method can measure directly and accurately.

facts.text: Recharge is hard to quantify because evaporation, transpiration and infiltration must first be measured or estimated to close the balance.
Common methods are chloride mass balance, soil physics methods, environmental and isotopic tracers, groundwater-level fluctuations, water balances and river baseflow.
Direct physical methods measure the water passing below the root zone; indirect ones infer recharge from soil physical parameters.
Numerical codes such as HYDRUS1D, UNSAT-H and SHAW use climate and soil data and some form of the Richards equation to model flow in the vadose zone.

definition.text: The natural or artificial removal of surface and subsurface water from an area that has too much of it.

facts.text: The internal drainage of most farm soils prevents severe waterlogging, but many soils need artificial drainage to raise production or to manage water supplies.
The Indus Valley Civilization had drainage systems, and every house in the major cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro had water and drainage.
The invention of hollow-pipe drainage is credited to Sir Hugh Dalrymple, who died in 1753.
Simple open drains, pipes and berms are still common, alongside larger earthworks and newer technologies.
Surface drains carry runoff from paved ground, while subsurface drains remove water seeping into the soil; gravel-filled French drains with perforated pipes are the commonest subsurface type.
Behind an impermeable retaining wall, undrained groundwater builds hydrostatic pressure that can crack the wall and wash out soil, leaving voids and sinkholes.
Most jurisdictions have a body of drainage law limiting how far a landowner may alter drainage from a parcel.

title: Agricultural land drainage

definition.text: Removing excess water from farmland, such as wetland soils or fields waterlogged for short spells, so that crops are not damaged.

facts.text: Glacial marshes in the northern United States and Europe were drained by ditches into mucklands used for high-value crops such as vegetables.
In the Netherlands, 15th-century windpumps drained only marginal land; the Haarlemmermeer had to wait for large steam pumps and was drained between 1849 and 1852.
Coastal plains and river deltas with high water tables need drainage for farming; Florida's flatwoods citrus groves are pumped after heavy rain.
Clay-rich soils pass water down very slowly, and hardpans or shallow rock block it, so roots suffocate when excess water shuts out air.
Even excellent soils waterlogged for a week of the year can lose their fruit trees.
Rice needs complete water control, as fields are flooded or drained at different stages of the crop.
Irrigation water carries salts that evapotranspiration concentrates, so irrigated land may need periodic over-irrigation and drainage to control salinity.
Subsurface drainage of acid sulfate soils is normally not advisable, but surface drainage can remove acidic chemicals in rainy periods and help reclaim them.

notes: S:96309007651c says draining the Haarlemmermeer created 'thousands of km2 of new land', which looks too large; the number is left out here for the verification pass.

definition.text: Synthetic fabrics used in drains to hold back fine soil particles while letting water through, so the drain does not clog.

facts.text: In a typical drain the fabric lines a trench filled with gravel, shells or stone, is folded over the top and covered with soil; groundwater seeps through it to an outfall.
Where groundwater is high, a perforated PVC or PE pipe along the base increases the volume the drain carries.
Prefabricated HDPE drains with geotextile, coco fibre or rag filters avoid hauling stone aggregate, which is always more expensive.

definition.text: Drainage designed to imitate the natural flow of water more closely than traditional piped systems.

facts.text: Seattle's Street Edge Alternatives Project uses roadside ditches, plantings and uncurbed sidewalks so runoff flows onto permeable ground.
Seattle Public Utilities reported a 99 percent reduction in storm water leaving the project.
Since 2010, UK local and neighbourhood planning has been required by law to factor such systems into development projects.

title: Waterlogging

definition.text: The saturation of soil with water, so that its air phase is restricted and anaerobic conditions prevail much of the time.

facts.text: All plants need oxygen to respire, and in farming waterlogging usually blocks air from reaching the roots.
Prolonged waterlogging brings anaerobiosis: roots of mesophytes suffer, and the reducing subsoil drives denitrification, methanogenesis and reduction of iron and manganese oxides.
Apart from rice, most crops, such as maize and potato, are highly intolerant of waterlogging.
Roots can survive by forming aerenchyma, switching to anaerobic metabolism and changing their architecture.
In irrigated land waterlogging often comes with salinity, because waterlogged soils prevent the leaching of salts brought in with irrigation water.
Badly run irrigation causes it on a large scale: over 2 million hectares are waterlogged on Pakistan's Indus Plains, and 2.19 million ha in Indian canal commands.

notes: Waterlogging (agriculture) is crawled but not assigned to any chapter; drafted here because Drainage links it repeatedly and it is mentioned on many in-scope pages.

definition.text: An equation relating the depth and spacing of parallel subsurface drains to the depth of the water table and the depth and hydraulic conductivity of the soil.

facts.text: The best-known steady-state form is Hooghoudt's drain spacing equation, derived from Darcy's law and introduced in the USA by van Schilfgaarde.
In steady state the water table stays level and drain discharge equals the recharge rate, a balance approximated by long-term seasonal averages.
From discharge, a permissible water-table depth, measured hydraulic conductivities and aquifer depth, it gives the design drain spacing for a chosen drain depth and radius.
Drainage criteria keep the water table neither too shallow, which cuts yields, nor too deep, which brings drought; in one example a seasonal average shallower than 70 cm depressed yield.

definition.text: The study of agricultural drainage systems and their effects, aimed at finding the best system design.

facts.text: Land drainage has agricultural, environmental, hydrological, engineering, economic, social and political aspects, all open to research, and aims at optimal farm production.
Water-table depth is a key criterion factor: drainage design controls it through drainage equations, and its relation to crop yield is optimized to set a drainage criterion.
Crop response rests on linked soil physical processes (aeration, structure, stability, temperature), chemical ones (salinity, acidity, alkalinity) and hydrological ones.
Irrigated land may need subsurface drainage to leach salts from irrigation water; leaching models such as SaltMod help set the drainage requirement.

definition.text: An instrument that measures the matric potential, or moisture tension, of water in unsaturated soil.

facts.text: It is a water-filled glass or plastic tube with a porous ceramic cup, topped by a vacuum gauge or by a rubber cap read with a needle instrument.
Buried and pumped to a partial vacuum, it gains vacuum as plants and evaporation dry the soil and loses it when the soil is rewetted.
Through the porous cup the water inside comes to balance with soil water, and the gauge then reads the soil's matric potential.
Irrigation managers use it to decide when to water and, with a water retention curve, how much.
Lorenzo A. Richards described its principles, construction and operation early in his career and kept improving the design.
ISO 11276:1995 sets out tensiometer methods for measuring pore water pressure in unsaturated and saturated soil.

definition.text: A device that estimates the volumetric water content of soil, usually indirectly from some other soil property.

facts.text: Instead of drying and weighing a sample, it reads a proxy such as electrical resistance, dielectric constant or interaction with neutrons.
The link between the proxy and moisture must be calibrated and can shift with soil type, temperature and electrical conductivity.
Technologies include frequency domain reflectometry, capacitance sensors, time domain reflectometry and transmission, neutron gauges, soil resistivity and galvanic cells.
Capacitance sensors resemble FDR sensors, which work at several hundred MHz, but run below 1 MHz and pick up more noise.
Soil water potential sensors, such as tensiometers and gypsum blocks, form a separate class measuring water potential instead of content.
Farmers use them to manage irrigation, using less water and raising yield and quality through better moisture control at critical growth stages.
Wired to an irrigation clock, a sensor makes a smart controller that skips watering when the soil is already wet.

title: Time-domain reflectometry

definition.text: A technique that sends an electrical pulse along a line and reads its reflections; in soil science it is used to measure the water content of soil and other porous media.

facts.text: Where the impedance along a conductor changes, part of the signal reflects back, and the time the pulse takes to return gives the distance to that change.
It works in soil because a material's permittivity, read from wave travel time, is closely tied to its water content, as Hoekstra and Delaney (1974) and Topp et al. (1980) showed.
Apparent permittivity comes from the travel time along two or more parallel metal rods in the soil, typically 10 to 30 cm long and linked to the instrument by coaxial cable.
Pulse velocity depends mainly on the permittivity of the medium, which varies greatly with moisture content and temperature.
Probes at several depths record when wetting arrives after rain starts, giving the speed of infiltration.
Outside soil science it locates faults in kilometre-long cables to within centimetres without digging them up.
A soil probe is a waveguide of two, three or more parallel wires fed voltage pulses by coaxial cable; slower pulse travel means wetter material.
Standard waveform analysis gives the average moisture along the probe; profile analysis methods add moisture at discrete points along it.

title: Capacitance probe

definition.text: A sensor that uses capacitance to measure the dielectric permittivity of the surrounding soil, and from it the soil's water content.

facts.text: Like a neutron probe, it sits in a PVC access tube in the soil, or comes as modular comb-like probes wired to a logger.
Two metal rings form capacitor plates with the soil as the dielectric between them; changes in soil permittivity shift the frequency of the oscillator circuit.
Water dominates the reading because its dielectric constant (80) is far above that of mineral soil (4), organic matter (4) and air (1).
The sensors oscillate at over 100 MHz in free air inside the access tube and are widely used for irrigation scheduling.

notes: Soil moisture sensor (S:e33f96551363) says 'so called capacitance sensors' run below 1 MHz; that describes PCB-type open-capacitor sensors, a different device from the access-tube probe here (over 100 MHz, S:5170a4b3e4a6). S:b7465f11e579 carries CITATION NEEDED.

definition.text: An instrument for measuring soil moisture in which the operating frequency of an oscillating circuit depends on the dielectric constant of the soil around it.

facts.text: Its types are capacitance probes and electrical impedance sensors.
Impedance sensors commonly feed a 100 MHz oscillator signal along a coaxial line into buried probe wires and measure the part reflected where impedance changes.
They are cheaper to build and respond faster than TDR, but the complex field around the probe means calibrating for each soil type, unless a high frequency is used.

definition.text: A NASA satellite that measures soil moisture and its freeze-thaw state across the planet.

facts.text: It takes a global snapshot of soil moisture every 2 to 3 days, often enough to see the effect of single storms as well as seasonal change.
Launched on 31 January 2015 with a passive L-band radiometer and an active radar, it lost the radar to an amplifier failure that year and carries on with the radiometer alone.
It senses the top 5 cm of soil through moderate vegetation, and hydrologic models extend the readings to infer moisture in the root zone.
Its data improve drought monitoring, flood and landslide forecasts, weather prediction and famine early warning.

definition.text: The practice of holding the water table at a chosen height by means of drainage.

facts.text: It is used on farmland, to raise crop yields with drainage systems, and in cities, to protect building foundations, underground transit and buried utilities.
Subsurface drainage keeps the water table of once-waterlogged land at a depth that suits its use; with drainage the water table lies deeper than without.
Crops differ in the water-table depth they tolerate, from 45 cm for wheat in the Nile Delta (very tolerant) to 90 cm for cotton there (sensitive).
A shallower permissible depth makes the system cheaper, but lowering the water table has side effects whose mitigation costs must also be counted.
Drainage began with shallow open ditches; around 1900 these gave way to buried clay tiles about 30 cm long, and from 1960 to corrugated plastic pipes laid by trenching machines.
Many large modern projects were over-designed and ignored environmental side effects, giving land drainage a poor reputation, partly through confusion with wetland reclamation.
Pumped wells give vertical drainage; used widely, with limited success, in Pakistan's Indus valley, they can be spaced over 1000 m apart, against 100 m or less for pipes and ditches.
Land drainage also helps control soil salinity, and the soil's hydraulic conductivity plays an important role in drainage design.

title: Available water capacity

definition.text: The amount of water a soil profile can store and make available to growing crops.

facts.text: It is also called available water content (AWC), profile available water (PAW) or total available water (TAW).
Frank Veihmeyer and Arthur Hendrickson defined readily available water as the difference between the water content at field capacity and at the permanent wilting point.
Plant-available water sits in pores of 0.1–75 μm; smaller cryptopores hold water too tightly for roots, and macropores are generally air-filled at field capacity.
Daniel Hillel argued that field capacity and wilting point were never clearly defined, lack a physical basis, and that water is never equally available across that range.
Lorenzo A. Richards called availability oversimplified: it depends both on roots absorbing water and on how readily soil water moves in to replace what they use.
Strongly alkaline, sodic soils have poor available water capacity, and thin rendzina soils have limited capacity.
Sepiolite clay can raise plant-available water in sandy soils.

contested_note: Hillel and Richards criticised the field-capacity-to-wilting-point definition as poorly defined and oversimplified.
notes: The criticism section heading is misspelt 'Critisism' on the page; S:bbe551fd9f9f (Hillel's proposed alternative) carries CITATION NEEDED and is not used.

definition.text: The unsaturated zone between the land surface and the water table, where water in the pores is below atmospheric pressure.

facts.text: Its water is held by adhesion and capillary action; where the zone lies in soil, that water is called soil moisture.
Its pores hold air as well as water, and it excludes the still-saturated capillary fringe just above the water table.
It is absent where there are lakes and marshes but can be hundreds of metres thick in arid regions.
Water flow through it is often described by the Richards equation, which rests partly on Darcy's law.
It often controls water movement from the surface to aquifers, so it governs recharge and whether, where and how fast contaminants reach groundwater.
Unlike the aquifers below, it is not a ready source of drinking water, but it supplies water and nutrients to the biosphere and is heavily used for crops, building and waste disposal.
Its study spans soil physics and hydrology and matters for agriculture, contaminant transport and flood control.

definition.text: Ground covered by water-resistant materials such as asphalt, concrete, brick or stone, mainly pavements and rooftops.

facts.text: Soils compacted by urban development are also highly impervious.
Paving seals the soil surface, ending rainwater infiltration and natural recharge, which can cause urban flooding; it also starves tree roots of air.
Cover rises with urbanization, from one or two percent in rural areas and about 10 percent in low-density suburbs to over 70 percent in industrial areas and over 90 percent in dense centres.
Porous pavements, green roofs and infiltration basins make urban structures behave more like pervious soils.

definition.text: Land usually classed as pervious that can still yield a substantial amount of surface runoff in small and large storms.

facts.text: It includes open water, wetlands, rock outcrops, barren ground and compacted soils.
Depending on conditions, it yields stormflow by infiltration-excess overland flow, saturation overland flow or direct precipitation.
Development compacts soils: Felton and Lull (1963) found a potential 80 percent cut in infiltration, and Taylor (1982) found construction cut infiltration rates by more than 77 percent.
Its effect on runoff matters more where total impervious area is low than in highly developed areas.

title: Total impervious area

definition.text: The share of an area covered by impervious surfaces, given as a fraction from zero to one or as a percentage.

facts.text: It is estimated from land-cover data in a GIS, land-use categories, percent developed area or population density; the US NLCD maps it in 30-metre pixels from 0 to 100 percent.
Percentage imperviousness (PIMP), an important factor in drainage, can be estimated as 6.4 times the square root of the number of dwellings per hectare.
PIMP is about 10% for woodland and 100% for dense commercial areas.
About 76 percent of the conterminous United States has less than 1 percent impervious cover.

notes: Facts draw on two sections (Total impervious area; Percentage imperviousness); the anchor is the larger one.

definition.text: The process irrigation managers use to decide how often and for how long to water.

facts.text: The aim is to wet the whole root zone while minimizing overwatering and keeping water use efficiency high.
Replenishing depleted water before stress sets in avoids moisture stress.
Methods range from watching plants for wilting and judging soil by feel, through sensors in the root zone, to soil water balance calculations.
Root-zone sensors include tensiometers, capacitance sensors and neutron probes, the last used for accurate deep readings.
Scheduling has moved from calendar timers to smart controllers that adjust to weather-based evapotranspiration or to measured soil moisture.
Soil-based controllers either skip a timed cycle when the soil is wet or start watering only when moisture falls to a set threshold.
The EPA WaterSense programme estimates that up to 50% of landscape water is wasted by inefficient methods.
Good scheduling prevents root rot and drought stress, and daily soil moisture estimates cut the risk of runoff and erosion.

title: Soil water balance method

definition.text: An irrigation scheduling method, also called the checkbook method, that tracks the water in the soil like a bank account.

facts.text: Rain and irrigation are the deposits; evapotranspiration, the soil's evaporation plus the plants' transpiration, is the withdrawal.
Each day's depletion equals the previous depletion plus crop evapotranspiration, minus rain and irrigation.
Crop evapotranspiration is reference evapotranspiration, the loss from a standard grass surface, adjusted by a crop coefficient set out in FAO Paper 56.
Coefficients above 1 mark high water users such as corn, and below 1 drought-tolerant plants such as cactus; the method relies on accurate weather data.

notes: The crop coefficient (Irrigation scheduling#Crop coefficient (Kc)) is folded in here rather than drafted as its own entry.

definition.text: The percentage of available soil water that can be used up before plants become stressed.

facts.text: It is often set at 50% for standard crops, 30% for sensitive crops such as vegetables, and 60–70% for stress-tolerant plants such as established trees.
Soil moisture sensors can act as a thermostat, triggering irrigation only when moisture drops below the threshold.

definition.text: A computer program that predicts the salinity of soil moisture, groundwater and drainage water, the water table depth and drain discharge in irrigated farmland.

facts.text: Developed by the Institute for Land Reclamation and Improvement (ILRI), it works from seasonal water balances, one to four seasons a year, to predict long-term trends rather than exact future states.
Most salinity models, such as Swatre and DrainMod, solve Richards' equation with hard-to-measure soil relations and daily data; SaltMod was built simpler, for field technicians and planners.
It tracks four reservoirs: the surface, the root zone, a transition zone that holds any horizontal drains, and the aquifer.
It can test drains at different depths, reuse of drainage and well water, and farmers' responses to waterlogging and salinity, which slow salinization toward an equilibrium.

title: Richards equation

definition.text: An equation describing the movement of water in unsaturated soils, published by Lorenzo A. Richards in 1931.

facts.text: It joins conservation of mass with the Darcy–Buckingham law for flow in variably saturated porous media, with a sink term that is usually root water uptake.
Although attributed to Richards, it was first introduced nine years earlier, in 1922, by Lewis Fry Richardson.
It is a quasilinear partial differential equation with analytical solutions only for particular conditions; existence and uniqueness of solutions were proved only in 1983, by Alt and Luckhaus.
Its mixed form has two unknowns, water content and pressure head, linked through the water retention curve.
It needs the soil's hydraulic properties: usually five van Genuchten retention parameters plus the saturated hydraulic conductivity.
It appears widely in environmental work because it describes flow in the vadose zone between the atmosphere and the aquifer.
Solving it numerically is among the hardest problems in earth science: solvers may fail to converge, and rain soaking into dry soil needs grid spacing under one cm near the surface.

notes: Priority: the page attributes the equation to Richards (1931) but says Richardson introduced it in 1922 (S:2a38172b0b5f); stated as a fact, not a value conflict.

title: Finite water-content vadose zone flow method
article: Finite water-content vadose zone flow method

definition.text: A one-dimensional alternative to the numerical solution of Richards' equation for simulating water movement in unsaturated soils.

facts.text: It solves the advection-like term of the soil moisture velocity equation as three ordinary differential equations, for infiltrating water, falling slugs and capillary groundwater.
Being explicit, it is guaranteed to converge, cheap to solve and mass-conserving, and it handles sharp wetting fronts that Richards solvers struggle with.
It assumes soil homogeneous in layers and omits soil water diffusion, which barely affects flux accuracy; in practice it is so far limited to one dimension.
It works with any monotonic retention and conductivity relations, such as Brooks and Corey or van Genuchten–Mualem.
