title: Ecohydrology

definition.text: An interdisciplinary field studying how water and ecological systems interact.

facts.text: It is a branch of hydrology with an ecological focus, covering both water bodies and land ecosystems such as forests and deserts.
Its research covers transpiration and plant water use, adaptation of organisms to water, vegetation effects on streams, and feedbacks between ecology, the soil carbon sponge and the water cycle.
A basic tool is the water balance at a point: water entering the soil equals water leaving plus the change in storage, through infiltration, evapotranspiration, deep leakage and runoff.
Where water is ample, as in rainforests, growth depends more on nutrients; in semi-arid savannas vegetation follows the water plants can draw from the soil.

notes: Ecohydrology#Vegetation and water stress overlaps Moisture stress, which the density-pores-and-compaction dossier owns, so no separate stress entry is drafted here.

definition.text: The blocking of soil pores by microbial cells and their byproducts, such as extracellular polymeric substance.

facts.text: The biomass forms an impermeable layer that sharply cuts infiltration, typically under continuous ponding in recharge ponds, irrigation channels, sewage systems, riverbeds and soils.
In continuously submerged soil, permeability first falls, then rises as trapped air dissolves, then falls for 2 to 4 weeks as aggregates break down and microbes clog the pores.
Gas bubbles such as methane from methanogens also clog pores; regular drying and pretreating water to cut suspended solids, nutrients and organic carbon reduce it.
It can help: it seals dairy wastewater ponds, cuts seepage from irrigation channels inoculated with algae and bacteria, and aids compacted clay landfill liners.

definition.text: An iron-rich, humus-poor mixture of clay with quartz and other minerals that forms as a redoximorphic feature in highly weathered soils.

facts.text: It forms in horizons saturated with water for part of the year, usually as dark red redox concretions in platy, polygonal or reticulate patterns.
Repeated wetting and drying, especially with heat from the sun, turns it irreversibly into ironstone hardpan or irregular aggregates; a single cycle does not.
It is firm near field capacity, hard below the permanent wilting point, and soft enough to cut with a spade when moist.
It marks Plinthosols, and though it can look like a mineral when hard, it is a pedogenic material.

definition.text: A knowledge base, proposed by McBratney et al. (2002), that infers soil properties to fill digital soil databases.

facts.text: It infers unknown properties with minimal uncertainty through logically linked pedotransfer functions.
Its premise is that a soil's basic properties are enough to infer all its other physical and chemical properties.
It depends on reliable inputs, links between basic soil data and quantified uncertainty, and computes new properties from inferred values as well as inputs.
A working prototype was completed in 2007–2009 at the University of Sydney with a US partner.

definition.text: A device that delivers a constant rate of flow from a closed bottle or tank.

facts.text: It is named after Edme Mariotte (1620–1684), but the design was first reported by McCarthy (1934).
An air inlet keeps the pressure at its base atmospheric, so a siphon at that depth delivers water at a constant head however far the reservoir level falls.
Constant head simplifies measuring water movement in soil; the Guelph permeameter and single and double ring infiltrometers use the principle.
It is sensitive to leaks at the air inlet and cannot be refilled while running; electronic devices now give accurate control.

definition.text: The percentage of water a soil retains against a centrifugal force 1000 times gravity, proposed in 1910 as a measure of field capacity for fine-textured soils.

facts.text: A saturated sample 1 cm thick is spun at 1000 times gravity for 30 min, and its gravimetric water content afterwards is the moisture equivalent.
Briggs and Shantz (1912) related it to texture: moisture equivalent = 0.02 sand + 0.22 silt + 1.05 clay.
Soil physics no longer uses the concept; field capacity has replaced it.

definition.text: The water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if water were not limited.

facts.text: It reflects the energy and wind available to move water vapour, the demand side of evapotranspiration, and is higher in summer, on clear or windy days and nearer the equator.
Actual evapotranspiration equals it when water is ample and can never exceed it.
Reference evapotranspiration (ET0) is calculated for a short-grass surface, most widely with the Penman–Monteith equation recommended by the FAO.
A crop coefficient and a stress coefficient convert reference evapotranspiration into actual crop evapotranspiration.

definition.text: The upper surface of the zone of saturation, the depth below which the ground is saturated with groundwater.

facts.text: Below it, pores and fractures are filled with groundwater; above it lies the unsaturated vadose zone.
It sits where water pressure equals atmospheric pressure; in soils with strong capillarity, water is drawn up above it as a capillary fringe.
It rises and falls with precipitation and evapotranspiration; in Britain or California it is lower in summer, and the band between levels is the zone of intermittent saturation.
It is rarely flat: its slope, the hydraulic gradient, depends on recharge, withdrawal and permeability.
Springs, rivers and lakes occur where it meets the surface, and groundwater inflow sustains their base flow.
A perched water table sits above the regional one on an impermeable or slowly permeable layer.
Most crops need a minimum depth to the water table: wheat in the Nile Delta tolerates 45 cm, while cotton there needs 90 cm.
The water level in a well tapping a confined aquifer marks a potentiometric surface, not the water table.

verification.evidence: Endosaturation.—A diagnostic soil characteristic consisting of a particular pattern of soil wetness characterized by saturated layers throughout the profile from a depth of 200 cm or more and extending upward to the top of the water table.
verification.note: the glossary's 200 cm is the depth in the endosaturation definition; the entry gives crop-tolerated water-table depths

definition.text: A soil-filled container, usually a cylinder, used to study how water and dissolved substances move through soil.

facts.text: It can hold an undisturbed soil monolith or rebuilt layers, carry probes at several depths, and collect leachate through an opening at the bottom.
Weighing lysimeters sit on scales, so weight changes give evaporation, transpiration and drainage, and hence actual evapotranspiration.
Suction lysimeters draw soil water through a buried porous cup under vacuum, and drainage lysimeters collect water passing through the profile to study leaching.
Edward Lewis Sturtevant built the first lysimeter in the United States in 1875.

definition.text: Lateral, unsaturated flow of water through the soil zone, typically in a permeable layer lying over a less permeable one.

facts.text: Infiltrated water still moves under gravity, sinking to the water table or, where permeability varies laterally, travelling downslope.
The water returns to the surface as return flow before or on entering a stream or groundwater.
Throughflow usually occurs during peak events such as heavy rain, at rates set by the hydraulic conductivity of the medium.
Bases left in a podzol's B horizon may be lost by throughflow.

definition.text: A field test of how fast soil absorbs water, made before building a septic drain field or infiltration basin.

facts.text: Holes are dug, presoaked for several hours, filled with water to a set level, and the fall in water level is timed as it soaks into the soil.
Results in minutes per inch are matched to local health codes to size the leach field.
Sandy soil generally absorbs more water than clay-rich soil or soil with a shallow water table.
Some jurisdictions doubt its accuracy and use soil texture analysis with long-term acceptance rates instead of or alongside it.

definition.text: The ability of an area of land to hold water in its pits and depressions so that it does not flow away.

facts.text: With infiltration capacity it governs Horton overland flow: once both are exceeded, water flows across the land, possibly causing flooding and soil erosion.
Its study matters in geology, ecology and especially hydrology.

title: Moisture stress

definition.text: A stress on a plant when the water in its tissues falls below optimal levels, because transpiration outpaces water uptake by the roots.

facts.text: It is described by two main metrics, water potential and water content.
Roots sensing dry soil make the hormone ABA, which closes stomata, cutting transpiration and photosynthesis, and loosens root cell walls so roots grow in search of water.
Irrigation scheduling avoids it by replacing depleted soil water before stress sets in; in strongly acidic soils, aluminium toxicity can cause it even when the soil is fairly moist.
Mildly stressed plants recover in 1–2 days, but after severe stress they regain only 40-60% of maximum photosynthesis the day after rewatering.

notes: A plant-physiology page assigned here by the graph; it fits Water in soil better.

definition.text: A measure of a liquid's pressure, normalized by its specific weight, plus its elevation above a datum, expressed as a length.

facts.text: It is measured as the height of the water surface in a piezometer or standpipe relative to a common datum.
Total head is pressure head plus elevation head, h = ψ + z, a simplified form of the Bernoulli principle for incompressible fluids.
For a 400 m deep piezometer at 1000 m elevation with water 100 m down, z = 600 m, ψ = 300 m and h = 900 m.
Each extra metre of fresh water adds about 9.8 kPa of static pressure.
The distribution of head decides where groundwater flows: where head is constant nothing flows, and a head difference drives water from higher to lower head.
Because water density varies with temperature and salinity, heads are standardized to fresh water head before they are compared.
Rising atmospheric pressure loads an aquifer and lowers well water levels, an effect described by USDA soil physicist Edgar Buckingham in 1907.

definition.text: The change in hydraulic head between measurement points along a flow path.

facts.text: Its magnitude, i = dh/dl, is the head difference divided by the flow path length between two piezometers, a dimensionless ratio.
In groundwater it is also called the Darcy slope, because it sets the size of the Darcy flux.
As a vector it gives both the size and direction of groundwater flow, which runs down the gradient from high to low head.
Combined with Darcy's law and a hydraulic conductivity tensor, it gives the flux of water in three dimensions.

definition.text: An underground layer of permeable, porous or fractured rock, or of unconsolidated gravel, sand or silt, that holds and yields water.

facts.text: Aquitards are low-permeability beds of clay or non-porous rock that restrict flow between aquifers; a completely impermeable one is an aquiclude or aquifuge.
Aquifers occur from near the surface to deeper than 9,000 m; shallower ones are more often used for water supply and irrigation and more readily refilled by local rain.
Despite the image of underground rivers or lakes, most aquifers are porous rock saturated with water.
Recharge, water moving down from the surface to the groundwater, is the main way water enters an aquifer.
In porous aquifers groundwater seeps slowly between sand grains; 0.3 m a day counts as a high rate.
Porosity alone does not make a good aquifer: rocks such as the Deccan Traps basalts are highly porous but poorly permeable.
Karst aquifers form where carbonic acid widens fissures in limestone; their fast flow makes them far more sensitive to contamination than porous aquifers.
Overdrafting, land subsidence, salinization and pollution are the main environmental problems of pumping groundwater from aquifers.

definition.text: The division of aquifers by whether an impermeable layer lies directly above them (confined) or their upper boundary is the water table (unconfined).

facts.text: Confined aquifers are usually capped by clay, which may give some protection from surface contamination.
Confined aquifers store water by matrix expansion and water compressibility, with storativities far below 0.01 and as low as 10−5.
Unconfined aquifers release water by draining their pores, with specific yields above 0.01, or 1% of bulk volume.
A perched aquifer is a small body of groundwater held above the regional aquifer on a low-permeability layer such as clay.

definition.text: Water held beneath the Earth's surface in the pore spaces of soil and rock and in rock fractures.

facts.text: About 30 percent of the world's readily available fresh water is groundwater.
In the technical sense it includes soil moisture, permafrost and immobile water in tight bedrock, not only water flowing in shallow aquifers.
Its natural input is infiltration that percolates down to the water table; its natural outputs are springs and seepage to the oceans.
It is a long-term store of the water cycle, with residence times from days to millennia.
In the Great Artesian Basin, groundwater travels about 1 metre per year and can be more than 1 million years old.
About 70% of extracted groundwater is used in agriculture.
Where salty water evapotranspires, salts are left behind; poor drainage in irrigation districts can raise water tables to the surface and cause soil salinity and waterlogging.
Pollution, often from improper waste disposal on land, forms plumes that spread by water movement and dispersion and is harder to clean up than surface water pollution.

definition.text: The saturated zone below the water table, in which all pores and fractures are filled with water.

facts.text: It is the counterpart of the unsaturated vadose zone above the water table.
Its size and depth fluctuate with the seasons and with wet and dry periods.
Depending on particle packing and porosity, its boundary can be stable or form unstable fingering patterns known as Saffman–Taylor instability.
Deep-rooted phreatophytes draw much of their water from the phreatic zone or near it.

definition.text: Lateral movement of water through the unsaturated zone that returns to the surface or enters a stream.

facts.text: It occurs when infiltrated water meets hydraulic conductivity that decreases with depth and flows downslope.
Throughflow is the part of interflow that returns to the surface as overland flow before reaching a stream or groundwater.
If the subsurface saturates, interflow may exfiltrate as return flow and become overland flow.
Interflow and soil piping can erode gullies as well as surface runoff.

definition.text: The flow of water beneath the Earth's surface as part of the water cycle.

facts.text: Water that infiltrates wets the vadose zone and recharges aquifers, and the excess moves on as subsurface runoff.
Its movement is set mainly by the water gradient, the type of substrate and barriers to flow.
Flow in the soil can be unsaturated, but faster subsurface flow goes with local saturation.
It returns to the surface at lower elevations through springs, seeps, wells or streams, sometimes after thousands of years in an aquifer.

definition.text: The scientific study of the movement, distribution and management of water on Earth, including the water cycle and water resources.

facts.text: It divides into surface water hydrology, groundwater hydrology (hydrogeology) and marine hydrology.
Its themes include infiltration, the process by which water enters the soil, part of which percolates down to the water table.
Soil moisture is measured by capacitance probe, time domain reflectometer or tensiometer, as well as by solute sampling and geophysical methods.
Ecohydrology, one of its branches, studies interactions between organisms and the hydrologic cycle.

definition.text: The branch of geology dealing with the distribution and movement of groundwater in soil and rock, mainly in aquifers.

facts.text: It covers the laws of subsurface water movement, the water's interaction with the porous solid, and the transport of energy, chemicals and particles by flow.
Groundwater hydrology and geohydrology are near-synonyms, though hydrogeology is the usual term.
The type of aquifer decides what controls flow: storativity for confined aquifers, specific yield for unconfined ones.
Darcy's law, derived by Henry Darcy in 1856, is its basic constitutive equation for groundwater discharge.

definition.text: The equation describing the movement of groundwater through a porous medium, known in mathematics as the diffusion equation.

facts.text: It is usually derived from Darcy's law combined with conservation of mass in a small control volume.
Fluid and matrix compressibility enter it; clay has a compressibility of 10−6 to 10−8 Pa−1 against 10−7 to 10−9 for sand.
The Theis and Thiem equations, its transient and steady-state solutions for flow to a well, are used in pumping tests.
The Hooghoudt equation applies it to subsurface drainage by pipes, tile drains or ditches.

definition.text: The principle that inflows to any water system equal its outflows plus the change in storage over a time interval.

facts.text: A system can be a soil column, a drainage basin, an irrigation area or a city; the balance is also called a water budget.
A general basin form is P = Q + ET + ΔS: precipitation equals streamflow plus evapotranspiration plus change in storage in soil or groundwater.
It rests on conservation of mass and assumes a closed system; water leaving to another basin must be accounted for.
Comparing budgets across areas quantifies how geology, soils, vegetation and land use affect the hydrologic cycle.
It is used in irrigation, runoff assessment, flood and pollution control and the design of subsurface drainage by pipes, tile drains, ditches or wells.
Monthly water balance models have been studied since the 1940s.

definition.text: The study of the water balance components involved in agricultural water management, especially irrigation and drainage.

facts.text: It divides the soil profile into reservoirs: the surface, the unsaturated root zone with mainly vertical flow, a transition zone, and the aquifer with mainly horizontal flow.
For the root zone, infiltration plus capillary rise equals actual evapotranspiration plus percolation plus the change in storage.
Bordering zones can be combined, and over months or years storage terms are often negligible, giving steady-state balances.
Its water balances also underpin the salt balances of irrigated land and models such as SaltMod and SahysMod.

definition.text: Calculating how much water a field needs from irrigation, and must lose through drains or wells, from its water balances.

facts.text: With surface evaporation neglected and actual evapotranspiration set to potential, the topsoil balance gives Irr = Epo + Osu + Per − Rai − Cap.
Irrigation efficiency is the fraction of irrigation water the crop consumes, Epo/Irr.
Subsurface and well drainage requirements, from drain or well discharge in the balances, are central to designing agricultural drainage systems.

In the Netherlands, 720 mm of precipitation against 540 mm of evaporation gives a winter drainage requirement of 180 mm; shallow-rooted pastures need summer irrigation, deep-rooted wheat practically does not.

definition.text: The movement of water through a plant and its evaporation from aerial parts such as leaves, stems and flowers.

facts.text: It is passive, costing the plant no energy, and also cools plants and drives the mass flow of mineral nutrients.
Only a small part of the water roots take up is used for growth; 97–99.5% is lost by transpiration and guttation.
Flow from soil to roots depends on the soil's hydraulic conductivity and the pressure gradient through the soil; flow up the plant is driven mainly by water potential differences.
When roots take up less water than leaves lose, stomata close, which slows nutrient uptake and limits photosynthesis and growth.
Soil temperature and moisture influence stomatal opening, and root uptake suffers in dry, very fertile or salty soils.
An acre of corn gives off about 3,000–4,000 U.S. gallons (11,000–15,000 liters) of water a day.
Isotope measurements show transpiration is the larger part of evapotranspiration, and that transpired water differs from groundwater and streams, so soil water is less well mixed than assumed.
It is measured with potometers, lysimeters, porometers, photosynthesis systems and sap flow sensors.

definition.text: The loss of rigidity of a plant's non-woody parts when turgor pressure in its cells falls towards zero for lack of water.

facts.text: It happens when the plant loses water faster than it absorbs it.
Soil causes include drought, high salinity drawing water from cells, and saturated soil that starves roots of oxygen so they cannot move water.
Plants may recover overnight as stomata close and evaporation falls, but permanent wilting kills the plant.
Wilting reduces water loss by exposing less leaf area but also curbs transpiration, reproduction and growth.

definition.text: An equation that estimates evapotranspiration from meteorological data in place of direct measurement.

facts.text: Penman published it in 1948 and Monteith revised it in 1965.
Its inputs include net irradiance, ground heat flux, vapor pressure deficit, air density and heat capacity, and atmospheric and stomatal conductance.
Stomatal conductance captures leaf area index, water stress and CO2, so the equation is sensitive to vegetation parameters.
The FAO recommends it, but errors against direct measurement can range from -9 to 40%.
In 1998 the FAO simplified it (FAO 56) to compute reference evapotranspiration in mm per day from radiation, temperature and wind at 2 m and vapor pressure deficit.
Stress coefficients cut the estimate for environmental stress, such as saturated soil starving roots of oxygen, dry soil causing wilt, and salinity.
GIS-linked hydrologic models such as SWAT estimate evapotranspiration with it.

definition.text: A simplified substitute for the Penman–Monteith equation that needs only radiation observations.

facts.text: It drops the aerodynamic terms and multiplies reference evapotranspiration by an empirical constant, α.
Observed evaporation over well-watered vegetation was 1.26 times the reference rate.
It assumes plants with abundant water; arid regions with high moisture stress are estimated to have higher α.

definition.text: The water a standard, well-watered grass surface would lose under current temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation, written ET0.

facts.text: FAO 56 defines it for a hypothetical crop 0.12 m tall with a surface resistance of 70 s m-1 and an albedo of 0.23, actively growing and adequately watered.
The FAO derived the Penman–Monteith equation for modelling it.
Multiplying it by a crop coefficient gives the evapotranspiration of unstressed plants, ET = Kc × ET0; a stress coefficient converts it to actual crop evapotranspiration.
Weather-based irrigation controllers calculate it to set watering.

definition.text: A plant property used to predict evapotranspiration, most simply the ratio of a crop's evapotranspiration to that of a reference crop, Kc.

facts.text: Kc varies through the season with growth stage, often following a trapezoidal or leaf area index curve.
Stress coefficients between 0 and 1, of which water stress (Kw) is the commonest, are multiplied in to reduce the estimate.
Kc can exceed 1 when the crop uses more water than the reference.
Irrigation scheduling multiplies ET0 by Kc to get the crop's actual water requirement, ETc.

definition.text: A micrometeorological technique that computes vertical turbulent fluxes of gases, heat and water vapour from high-frequency wind and concentration data.

facts.text: The flux is the covariance between fluctuations of vertical wind speed and of gas concentration, times mean air density.
It is used over natural ecosystems and agricultural fields to measure water loss and evapotranspiration, carbon dioxide and methane exchange.
The source area of the measured eddies, the flux footprint, changes with wind direction, stability and measurement height.
It assumes flat, uniform terrain and fully turbulent flow, and needs instruments sampling at 5 to 40 Hz.

definition.text: An extremely thin layer of water, a few molecules thick, held on mineral surfaces.

facts.text: Water molecules are strongly polar, so they bond to each other and to charged surfaces such as soil minerals.
Clay is especially able to bond water molecules.
Bound water is much less mobile than the rest of soil water and strongly affects soil dielectric permittivity and freezing and thawing.

definition.text: The dependence of a soil's water content at a given matric potential on whether the soil is wetting or drying, that is, on its saturation history.

facts.text: The matric potential–water content relationship is the basis of the water retention curve.
At a matric potential of 5 kPa, a fine sandy soil could hold anywhere between 8% and 25% volumetric water.
Some matric potential sensors show hysteresis within the sensor itself, yet as of 2002 usually only desorption curves were measured in calibration.

definition.text: The height of a liquid column corresponding to the pressure the liquid exerts at its base, expressed as a length.

facts.text: Combined with elevation head it makes up hydraulic head.
Below the water table pressure head exceeds atmospheric pressure; the water table is where it equals atmospheric pressure.
Above the water table pressure head is negative and water partly filling the pores is under suction.
Because it is proportional to pressure for a given fluid, columns of water or mercury are used to measure pressure.

definition.text: A relation giving the pressure drop of a fluid flowing through a packed bed of solids, and from it the bed's permeability.

facts.text: Kozeny derived it in 1927 and Carman modified it in 1937 and 1956, modelling the bed as curving tubes with Poiseuille flow.
Permeability rises with particle diameter squared and with the cube of porosity, and falls with (1 − porosity) squared.
It is a special case of Darcy's law and holds only for creeping flow, with particle Reynolds numbers up to about 1.0.

definition.text: The hydraulic conductivity of a soil that is not saturated, which depends on its water content.

facts.text: Its dependence on water content is a main complication in studying the vadose zone.
It enters the Richards equation as K(h) and the soil moisture velocity equation as K(θ).
Relations such as Brooks and Corey, Clapp and Hornberger and van Genuchten–Mualem describe it, with parameters from the water retention curve.
The Guelph permeameter measures it in the field using a Mariotte bottle to keep a constant head.

definition.text: Systems that drain water on or in the soil to improve crop production, combining stormwater, erosion and water table control.

facts.text: The two main types are surface drainage and subsurface drainage.
Field systems control the water table, while main systems collect, carry and dispose of the water through an outlet.
Surface systems reshape the land into bedded systems on flat land or graded systems on slopes, draining by gravity.
Subsurface field drains can be open ditches, filled trenches, pipe, tile or mole drains, or wells, which are called vertical drainage.
Modern pipe drains are perforated PE or PVC wrapped in a filter envelope that keeps soil out, especially important in fine sandy and silty soils.
Checked or controlled systems use gates or pumping to drain only when needed, saving irrigation water; in northwestern India this did not cause undue salinization.
Surface drainage suits flat land with low-infiltration soils or intense rain; subsurface drainage suits shallow water tables.
Where saline groundwater lies deep, shallow closely spaced drains are better because deeper systems yield saltier effluent.

title: Tile drainage

definition.text: An agricultural drainage system of buried pipes that removes excess subsurface water from fields, leaving air space in the soil and firm ground for machinery.

facts.text: The name comes from its original fired-clay tiles; today HDPE and PVC tubing are common, though concrete and ceramic tiles are still used.
Short earthenware pipes were first laid in England in 1843; older land drains were stone-lined tunnels in clay soils and peats, laid deep enough to escape the plough.
Water enters through gaps between tile sections or perforations in plastic tile and usually ends up in lower-lying streams, rivers or lakes.
Lowering the water table keeps oxygen in soil pores, letting roots grow deeper and use water and nutrients better.
Sandy soils need little tiling, while clay soils hold water tightly and need lines closer together.
Perforations tend to clog with silt; gravel and geotextile surrounds slow this, but all land drains eventually fail.
Tree roots enter tile lines, so some farmers must clear them every year.
Flashboard risers in outlets can hold water in the root zone, controlling drainage and storing water for the crop.

definition.text: The effects of widespread tile drainage on wetlands, rivers and water quality.

facts.text: Draining wetlands caused population declines in hundreds of thousands of wetland species.
By moving water off the land faster, tile drainage delivers higher volumes to rivers, causing bank erosion and heavy sediment loads.
It can reduce erosion and phosphorus runoff, since soil filters water before it reaches streams, but its outflow tends to be very high in nitrogen.
Controlled drainage or constructed wetlands may work better than surface conservation practices on tile-drained land.

definition.text: Capillary action is a liquid flowing in a narrow space without help from external forces such as gravity.

facts.text: It arises from surface tension, caused by cohesion within the liquid, combined with adhesive forces between the liquid and the wall of a small enough tube or pore.
In a narrow tube water forms a concave meniscus; the contact length scales with the tube radius while the liquid weight scales with its square, so narrower tubes lift a liquid higher.
Jurin's law gives the rise height, which falls as tube radius increases: for water at 20 degrees C the rise is 0.7 mm in a 2 cm radius tube and 70 mm in a 0.2 mm radius tube.
In hydrology it describes attraction of water to soil particles; differences in soil matric potential drive it, moving water from wet to dry soil.
With mercury and glass the liquid's internal forces exceed those to the solid, giving a convex meniscus and a reversed capillary effect.
Where a high water table meets strong evaporation, capillary rise brings salts to the surface, and breaking capillary pores is used to stop it.

definition.text: Adhesion is the tendency of dissimilar particles or surfaces to cling to one another, whereas cohesion is that of like particles.

facts.text: Adhesion requires energy from chemical or physical linkages; the physical ones are reversible when enough energy is applied.
Proposed mechanisms are mechanical, chemical (ionic, covalent, hydrogen bonds), dispersive (van der Waals forces), electrostatic and diffusive.
In surface science adhesion almost always means dispersive adhesion; a low contact angle indicates higher adhesion per unit area.
Strength depends on the mechanisms present and contact area; liquids that wet a surface make larger contact.

definition.text: Capillary pressure is the pressure difference between two immiscible fluids in a thin tube or pore, arising from forces between the fluids and the solid walls.

facts.text: The Young-Laplace equation gives it as pc = 2 γ cos θ / r, with interfacial tension γ, wetting angle θ and effective radius r of the interface; the smaller the pore, the larger the pressure.
The wetting phase is the fluid that preferentially spreads across the walls; its wettability depends on surface tension and contact angle and can be changed by surface roughness or hydrophilicity.

In the porous plate method a water-saturated sample sits on a saturated plate in a gas chamber; gas pressure is raised, the gas pressure represents capillary pressure and the water expelled gives the saturation.
Beskow defined soil moisture tension as capillary pressure and soil water as capillary water, in his work on frost heave.

definition.text: A continuity equation describes the transport of a quantity, and is a local form of a conservation law.

facts.text: It relates change of a quantity in a region to net flux through the boundary plus generation (sources) or removal (sinks) inside.
In fluid dynamics it says the rate at which mass enters a system equals the rate it leaves plus the mass accumulating within.

definition.text: The Hagen-Poiseuille equation gives the pressure drop for an incompressible Newtonian fluid in laminar flow through a long cylindrical pipe of constant cross section.

facts.text: It assumes laminar flow in a circular pipe much longer than its diameter, no acceleration, and an incompressible Newtonian fluid.

Above a threshold of velocity and pipe diameter flow becomes turbulent, giving larger pressure drops than the equation predicts; it also fails near the pipe entrance and for low viscosity or wide, short pipes.
It was derived experimentally by Poiseuille (1838) and Hagen, and justified theoretically by Stokes in 1845.

definition.text: Horton overland flow is water flowing across the land surface when rainfall exceeds both infiltration capacity and depression storage capacity.

facts.text: It is named for Robert E. Horton, the engineer who first studied it in detail, and is also called Hortonian or unsaturated overland flow.
The flow is shallow, sheetlike and fast, so it can erode soil extensively, especially on steep terrain and loose, flat farmland.
Impermeable paved surfaces reach it rapidly, and it is common on construction sites and unpaved roads where vegetation has been stripped.
It is also called Hortonian overland flow, after Robert E. Horton, or unsaturated overland flow.

definition.text: Hygroscopy is the attracting and holding of water molecules from the surroundings by absorption or adsorption.

facts.text: Hygroscopic substances include many fertilizer chemicals and salts; the moisture held is usually proportional to relative humidity.
Deliquescent materials absorb enough water to dissolve into a solution, at a characteristic deliquescence relative humidity that depends on temperature and crystalline hydrate form.
Soil voids stay saturated with water vapour up to the point of maximal hygroscopicity, beyond which a vapour-pressure deficit develops in the pore space.

definition.text: Osmosis is the net movement of solvent through a selectively permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration, equivalently from high to low water potential.

facts.text: Osmotic pressure is the external pressure needed to stop net solvent flow; it is a colligative property, depending on the solute's molar concentration and not its identity.
Osmotic transport is a pressure-driven viscous flow of solvent, not random molecular diffusion.
Osmotic entry of water raises plant-cell turgor pressure until it equals the osmotic pressure; in a hypertonic solution water leaves and the cell shrinks, in a hypotonic one it swells turgid.
Roots take in water and nutrients across cell membranes by osmosis, so excess soil salt lowers water uptake and can cause leaf burn.

definition.text: Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom in a bent, polar molecule.

facts.text: A water molecule can make up to four hydrogen bonds, which explains its unusual thermodynamic properties compared with similar molecules.
Cohesion from hydrogen bonds and adhesion from polarity give high surface tension (71.99 mN/m at 25 degrees C) and capillary action, lifting water over 100 m in trees.
Specific heat capacity is very high at 4184 J/(kg K) at 20 degrees C, with a high heat of vaporization of 40.65 kJ/mol, both due to hydrogen bonding.
Density peaks at 3.98 degrees C, an unusual negative thermal expansion between 0 and 3.98 degrees C.
Water is an excellent solvent because of its high dielectric constant; hydrophilic substances dissolve while hydrophobic ones do not.
Long-term action of water on rock causes weathering and erosion that turn rock and minerals into soil and sediment.

definition.text: Surface tension is the energy per unit area that comes from a liquid having a surface, equivalently a force per unit length.

facts.text: Molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally in all directions, but surface molecules are pulled inward, so the surface contracts toward the smallest area.
Surface tension is a property of a liquid's interface with another medium, not of the liquid alone.
Surface tension falls as temperature rises and reaches zero at the critical temperature, so a stated value needs its temperature.
A curved liquid surface can balance a pressure difference across it, which is the basis of capillary effects.

definition.text: Gravitational water is the water that moves through the large soil pores and drains away under gravity.

facts.text: Gravitational water is the difference between the moisture content at saturation and at field capacity.
It drains from macropores too fast for plants to use.

definition.text: Capillary water is the water held in small soil pores by adhesion and cohesion.

facts.text: Only part of the capillary water in a soil is available to plants.
Plant available water is held between field capacity and the permanent wilting point, in mesopores.

definition.text: Hygroscopic water is the thin film of water held on soil particles between the hygroscopic coefficient and the oven-dry state.

facts.text: The hygroscopic coefficient is reached when the last micropore is drained and only films of water surround the particles.
Air-dry soil holds water at potentials of -3000 to -10,000 kPa, in equilibrium with pore air at about 98% relative humidity.
Soil dried at 105 degrees C to constant weight is oven dry, and the oven-dry weight is the reference for expressing water in mineral soils.
Unavailable water, held at the wilting point, is mostly hygroscopic water held too tightly in micropores for plants.

definition.text: Available water-holding capacity estimates the water held between field capacity and permanent wilting point in the rooting zone, or the top 150 cm if no layer limits roots.

facts.text: Water is summed horizon by horizon; a horizon unfavorable to roots, and every horizon below it, is left out of the total.
Each horizon's thickness is multiplied by a texture factor, for example 0.20 cm/cm for silt loam, and by the fraction not occupied by rock fragments.
A 25 cm silt loam A horizon with 10% rock fragments holds 25 x 0.20 x 0.90 = 4.50 cm of available water.
Profile totals fall into four classes: up to 7.5 cm, up to 15.0 cm, up to 22.5 cm, and above 22.5 cm of water.
Materials unsuited to roots include bedrock, fragipans, densic materials, and horizons cemented across 90% or more of the profile.

definition.text: Total porosity is the percent of soil volume that is pores, found as 100% minus bulk density divided by particle density times 100.

facts.text: The bulk density over particle density term is the percent of soil volume taken by solids; bulk and particle density must use the same units.
Porosity is the pore volume over total volume (solids plus pores) times 100.
Clayey soils usually have more total pore space than sandy soils, yet sandy soils have larger individual pores, so pore size distribution matters as much as total porosity.

definition.text: Soil water content is expressed either by weight, as gravimetric water content, or by volume, as volumetric water content.

facts.text: Gravimetric content is the mass of water divided by the oven-dry mass of soil, not the wet mass, times 100.
Bulk density converts between the two: a soil of bulk density 1.5 g/cm3 with 30% water by weight holds 45% water by volume.
Volumetric content describes the moisture around growing roots more realistically, and times soil depth it gives depth of water.
A 25 cm soil layer at 20% volumetric water holds 5 cm of water.

definition.text: Vapor flow is soil water movement driven by gradients in vapor pressure rather than water tension.

facts.text: The lab manual classes soil water movement as saturated flow, unsaturated flow and vapor flow.
Vapor flow is like capillary flow, but it moves along vapor pressure gradients.

definition.text: A soil water relationship is a graph of a sensor's measured value against soil water content, which acts as a calibration for one soil.

facts.text: Any soil moisture sensor reading must be interpreted through such a relationship.
Once calibrated, sensors quantify plant available water and show whether water flows by gravity, capillarity or osmotic potential.
At a given water potential, soil water content rises with clay content because clayey soils have higher porosity and hold more water.

definition.text: Soil pores hold water, air and organisms, and their shares shift as the soil wets and dries.

facts.text: In saturated soil gas exchange is very slow: respiration carbon dioxide cannot escape and oxygen cannot enter, giving anaerobic conditions.
A soil with little water has good gas exchange but may not supply enough water to plants and organisms.
Gravity pulls water down while capillarity holds it in pores through adhesion to solids and cohesion between water molecules, strongest in small pores.
A well-aggregated loam balances large pores for drainage and aeration with small pores for water storage between rains.
Such soil also infiltrates water well, which raises plant water availability and cuts runoff and erosion.

definition.text: Pore size sets how much water a soil keeps after free drainage, so texture and aggregation shape the field capacity water content.

facts.text: Like a saturated sponge that stops dripping, a soil reaches field capacity after about two days of free drainage following heavy rain or irrigation.
Coarse sand drains fast through large pores, so its field capacity is low and little water is left for plants before wilting.
Rapidly draining sands also lose dissolved nitrate and pesticides more readily than fine loams and clays.
A dense compacted clay loam has mainly small pores and a high field capacity; prolonged saturation causes anaerobic problems such as denitrification losses.

definition.text: Plant water availability depends both on how much water the soil retains and on how much soil roots can reach.

facts.text: Water retention depends on texture, aggregation and organic matter, while rooting volume is strongly affected by compaction.
A compacted horizon may hold enough water, yet roots cannot penetrate most of it, so the plant cannot get the moisture and nutrients it needs.
Corn in subsoiled soil rooted about twice as deep as corn limited to the plow layer by a plow pan.
Alfalfa needs much water and its taproot reaches deep; vineyards and wheat need much less.

definition.text: Infiltration capacity is the maximum amount of rainwater that can enter a soil in a given time.

facts.text: It depends on soil type, with large pores giving higher capacity, on structure, and on moisture at the start of the rain.
Runoff is produced when rainfall exceeds infiltration capacity; in a long intense storm the wetting soil takes water more slowly.
Sandy and gravelly soils keep infiltrating better in a storm than fine loams and clays, but well-aggregated fine soils can also keep high rates until aggregates fail and compaction sets in.
Frozen ground blocks pores with ice and poorly aggregated soils have few open large pores, so both raise runoff and erosion risk.

definition.text: Soil strength changes with moisture: saturated soil is soft and erodible, moist soil is firm, and very dry sandy soil is loose.

facts.text: Supersaturated soil has no internal strength because positive pore water pressure pushes particles apart, so it erodes easily or slides as mud.
In moist soil, curved pore-water surfaces touching solids pull particles together, making the soil firmer and harder.
In very dry low-organic soils, especially sands, no pore water holds particles together, so wind can lift them.
Strong aggregation gives extra cohesion at these moisture extremes and is kept up by organic inputs, roots, mycorrhizal hyphae, mulch and less tillage.

definition.text: Annual amount, seasonal timing, and the intensity, duration and frequency of rain all affect crop production and losses of water, sediment and contaminants.

facts.text: Water shortage is the most significant yield-limiting factor worldwide; regular gentle showers are better than infrequent intense storms that cause runoff and erosion.
With excess water the main problem is the lack of air exchange and oxygen.
Subsurface drainage and raised beds remove excess water, irrigation overcomes shortage, and rice allows grain on poorly drained soil.
Good soil management makes soils and crops more resilient to weather extremes, a lesson of the 1930s Dust Bowl.
